newsitem.title: USA: Fed nominees unlikely to alter U.S. credit policy.
newsitem.headline: Fed nominees unlikely to alter U.S. credit policy.

text.p: The nomination of two new members to the Federal Reserve Board of governors is unlikely to produce any major short-term impact on the way the central bank conducts monetary policy, Fed watchers said.

"The Fed is now in a holding pattern and I think these new guys, as a result, will fit right in with that view," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director of the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington-based think tank.
"So I don't think it's going to affect policy at the short-term at all," he added.

President Bill Clinton announced on Thursday he would nominate Edward Gramlich and Roger Ferguson to fill the two vacant seats at the Fed Board. The formal announcement was widely expected by the political and financial communities.

Gramlich, an economist at the University of Michigan, and Ferguson, a partner with consulting firm McKinsey & Co., are not expected to face any major resistance in Congress, analysts said. If the U.S. Senate confirms the nominations of the two economists, Clinton will have named five of the seven members of the Fed Board.

In the long run, economists said, the new members, if confirmed, is likely to tilt the Fed Board a little toward the dovish, pro-growth side rather than the hawkish, kill-inflation-before-it-takes-root side.

"There will probably will a slight bias towards letting the economy go on without tightening (policy) and making sure it grows enough to absorb all the people coming into the labor force," Chimerine said.
Wall Street analysts said, however, such a phenomenon should come as no surprise since Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan is mostly seen as having adopted a more pro-growth monetary policy already.
"There has been a pro-growth shift in the Board already and these two new appointees would perhaps slightly re-inforce that," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston Co Inc.
From a general perspective, analysts said the two Clinton nominees are seen as moderate, slightly dovish economists.
"These two are very middle-of-the-road type of guys," said a senior economist at a large Wall Street financial firm.
While Gramilich appears to be more well known in Washington and Wall Street, Ferguson's opinions on monetary policy are seen as more of a mystery, analysts said.

"Gramilich is a consesus builder, not insistant on his own point of view. He's going to fit in very well. Now Ferguson is still a bit of a mystery to me. But I've been told he is a very moderate type of economist," the senior economist added.
The current members of the Fed board are - Alan Greenspan, Chairman; Alice Rivlin, Vice Chair; Laurence Meyer, Governor; Susan Philips, Governor; and Edward Kelley, Governor.
Greenspan, Rivlin and Meyer are Clinton's appointees. Chairman Greenspan was first appointed by President Ronald Reagan, re-appointed by President George Bush and re-appointed again by Clinton.
Philips was nominated by Bush in 1991 and Kelley was first nominated by Reagan and then re-appointed by Bush.

The Fed last changed rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The Fed left rates steady during the May 20 and the July 1-2 meetings of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
